Original, and that is something missing in today's game world.

But original does not automatically means good.

It's like reading a book, with a story that does not hook you up in any way. And in order to read the story, you need to go through many useless paragraphs in order to find the few pieces of text that are actually pertinent for the very ordinary story.

Or like Facebook, where its hard to find the few interesting pieces mixed up into all the useless posts. At least, on Facebook, it's about peoples that you know. Here, it's about uninteresting characters.

You are drawn in by curiosity for the first hour. It becomes boring as you go along in the second hour. You have something better to do after that.
Big brother is watching. This is more of a conspiracy game than siblings, but I enjoyed it anyway.

No spoilers here; this a story-focused game so you're better off playing it blind your first runthrough.

Orwell is an interesting cousin of a visual novel. There are a couple of time-sensitive (you'll have to figure out your options from context clues) events and alas, you can't fastforward through conversations until they take place in "real-time", but overall, you can move through the game at your own pace. If you're the type of gamer who enjoys reading and storycrafting, there's enough optinal reading material in the game to give you a sense of who these characters you're spying on were in the past and who they have become now. There's also some chuckle-worthy materials like GYM interviews, typical internet trolls and sheeple, etc. All in all, Orwell's digital world feels real... until you get the clues wrong and the hard plot "corrects" itself at the end of each chapter. But you ARE in charge of the soft plot (characters' fate, government opinion, etc.). You'll probably need a couple of run-throughs before you realize you had options on what to do with the information you uncover that you didn't think of before. You can enjoy the multiple branching storylines (though the main story remains the same) a few times (maybe 30-40 minutes per chapter on your first play, depending how much you like reading then 20 minutes per chapter in your later playthroughs) before getting everything Orwell has to offer and wish you had some more. In which case, there's a full sequel out now (April 2018)!

tl;dr Enjoyable game with a hit-or-miss art style, lots of clicking, good story-building with a couple of good twists, atmospheric music that lets you know when you found something game-changing, interesting commentary about government surveillance.

The reason this review is "Positive" is that there's not "Meh" button, and I don't want to hate on things for no reason, either.

The message is pretty much predictable, and while you might have certain doubts/hopes in the beginning that there will be arguments for both sides - spoilers - well, there are none.

UI is a little clunky, the characters are mostly annoying stereotypical millenials, and, frankly, fuck me for spending 5 hours on it, I do have - simply more fun - things to do in my life. But, funnily enough, I felt compelled to finish it, so then again, maybe it's not so bad?..

I guess it has something to do with a Bad TV Show syndrome - it's mediocre, but once you're in, there's an itch inside to see the story through. The story is meh-ish, and kind of weird: the 'big' plot twist is...well...real bad, i'll just leave it at that, while there's a certain number of small unexpected things that are implemented...just really well, as in you don't see them coming, and in the same time they fit the story really well.

That all said, I have no idea why there's a season 2, except for the dev wanting more monies, especially having seen the ending(s) and all.
Is there something wrong with it? - No.
Will I be playing season 2? - oh fuck no.

Orwell stars you, the player, as an investigator in the Nation's (a stand-in for an unholy almagamation of the United States and the United Kingdom) new, government-ordained spying programme. Your job is to investigate suspected terrorists and cherrypick data you've acquired via researching the Internet and spying directly on their conversations, phones, and computers. You upload these data modules to the Orwell database and help construct a profile of these suspects that your advisor (who can't see your research sources in an effort to maintain some sort of ethical loophole) then uses to report back to the authorities, thus causing your actions to have potentially devastating consequences.

I've seen a few people complain about the gameplay--you are, essentially, dragging these data modules from one part of your screen to another (and, frustratingly, it can take a few clicks to get hold of them), which sounds unexciting on paper. But the story is compelling, and it's through this (slightly repetitive and boring) gameplay that you unlock the story, which can branch depending on which data you upload to Orwell. Some of it you have to, some of it you don't--and some of it you can use to alter the perception of certain suspects by picking which element of contradicting data you want to show to the advisor. 

The game does a very good job of highlighting how people become complacent with this level of privacy invasion--I've seen complaints of the game handholding you throughout, but, in my opinion, this helps you to slip into the mindset of uploading whatever data you come across, mindlessly painting suspects as victims because it's what your advisor wants of you. It wasn't until the end of my first playthrough that I realised how much damage I'd caused by providing evidence to suggest that innocent people were guilty of crimes they hadn't committed, and how many of the characters I'd either had arrested or killed via my actions of "innocuously" collecting their data. Which I guess is what the game wants you to do, particularly on a first playthrough.

That's not to say I don't have complaints. The game wants you to play multiple playthroughs, even if only to collect all of the achievements (most of which can be acquired in two playthroughs; two require a third, or replaying chapters on one of your profiles). Different actions have different outcomes and dialogue, and that produces slightly new scenes to watch (or, really, read). The problem is that the texts and calls you have to monitor can be so tediously long, particularly with little deviation--the last chapter has one that's just about shy of 10 minutes, and you can't do anything but sit and let it play. There's no option to skip the scene. 

I've also seen a few people complain that the game thinks people can never lie or exaggerate, which I assume refers to options where you can report suspects for having outspoken anti-government tendencies... but again, I think this is overlooking what the game wants you to consider. 

I highly recommend Orwell, although I bought it in the Humble Bundle and so bought it for much cheaper than its standard price--and I've already collected all the achievements in just over 6 hours of play, which isn't quite a £1 = 1 hour of playtime at its normal price. It's obviously not a game that's appealing to everyone, but I do think for those that like immersive visual novels with political themes (and that's essentially what it is), you'll enjoy Orwell.

Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

In this game you take the role of a CIA agent in 2012 using the tool that was leaked by Edward Snowden, XKeyScore. 

Your tasked with getting the guys responsible for 3 terrorist acts in jail. You quickly stumble upon a group called The Thot. Everyone in it is clearly a terrorist and should've been arrested decades ago. The whole game you are wondering what's taking your supervisor so long to finally arrest the fools. 

So i finally get to the end of act 5. I identified the 3 terrorists: Everyone in the thot group, the supervisor woman (Sykes was cool, the woman is clearly shady), and the owners of the pharmaceutical company. I couldn't get the supervisor arrested nor the pharmaceutical owners. But luckily everyone in thot was jailed. Good. Then for whatever reason they wanted me arrested. Very cool experience! I hesitate to call it a game because there isn't much in the way of gameplay here. It's more of a choose-your-own-adventure book or interactive experience. If you don't like reading, don't bother with this game. There is no voice acting, and the "gameplay" is basically dragging pictures and text between windows. 

However, I still couldn't stop playing it once I got going. The story is interesting with a bunch of twists and turns, and I really did feel like an investigator hunting for clues. I enjoyed filling-in people's database entries and connecting the clues and building a collection of information.

There were times when I was a little frustrated because I felt like information was relevant to the case, but the game wasn't programmed to let me highlight it, but for the most part it was matched up pretty well to what I thought was relevant.

Also, there are branching storylines and multiple endings, but it would have been nice if there were more options to stray from the linear story based on what you highlight in investigations. However, I'm sure that would have been too much for a small team and indie-developer to flesh out, so I'm pretty satisfied with how it is now.

I didn't find the game overly preachy, maybe just a little at the very end. It's obvious what they're going for from the name of the game alone, but I thought it was presented in an interesting and clever way.

Definitely a recommend from me, as something to experience once.

My opinion on the ethical problems presented (Spoilers):
[spoiler]Abraham was an idiot for wanting a human element included in Orwell. Humans are biased and flawed creatures,
 so it should have been obvious from the beginning that an investigator could tailor the information that the advisor receives in order to affect their viewpoint. I am honestly at a loss that the directors behind the project could think that adding another human (the evaluator) into the process would improve the project's capabilities.

Another thing which bothered me: by it's nature, Orwell is reactive instead of proactive. While clearly there weren’t any problems in adding people to be investigated, people were only investigated if they were connected with someone who was a suspect. Which by nature meant that potential domestic terrorists who are radicalized simply through hardship in their life are never investigated (Think Nina, but without involvement in Thought).

I think that some kind of AI / massive neural network could do a much better job and might actually work in preventing terrorism by catching threats before they are realized.
Also, to expand on that, I believe that instead of locking up "potential" terrorists, The Nation should prioritize helping them instead. [/spoiler]

Orwell strives to put you in a situation that might be possible in the real world. A world in which not only is everyone being watched, but one in which a wrong word here or a something taken out of context could easily land you in jail for a crime you never commited. Your heart strings and moral compass will be pushed and pulled. Who should you believe? Did this person really do what others seem to claim, or are they an innocent? You'll see the good and bad in every person including yourself. Every choice you make could lead to radically different outcomes. A seemingly right choice here could lead to the deaths of many, or a dark future. You can't know the effects your choices will make, but that's what makes it fun and brings you back again and again. What would happen if I made this choice instead of this one here? What consquences will it lead to? Overall Orwell is a fantastic game worth your money and your time. You'll grow to love the story and come back again and again to see what different outcomes. What will happen, only you can decide.

If you've ever watched the TV show Person of Interest... it's kind of similar to that show except all the data analysis is done by an incredible artificial intelligence rather than human analysts. Orwell is basically why human analysts are redundant when an artificial intelligence overlord take over intelligence gathering.

In this game you're basically a graduate data analyst working for a secret government organisation, tasked to monitor all electronic communications and data packets on the internet. Orwell is an electronic data warehouse used to store information on relevant persons of interest. It is up to you to collate the information, then escalate your POI assignments to a senior analyst, who happens to be a narrator and guides you through a series of unfortunate plot events. 

At times they game is like watching grass grow. It suffers from terrible pacing and is kind of like my job in real life... except I actually get paid by the hour to watch the incredibly boring slide show. You will spend multiple hours mindlessly clicking at links on the screen.

By chapter three i got really tired of the mundane plot and really wondered why I stuck it out for three hours.

If you enjoy watching paint dry, this might be the game for you. Otherwise... bury it at the very bottom of your list of games to play.

[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

As a rule I hate story-focused games with little to no gameplay. But this one... I'm very much interested in totalitarian, dystopian and, well, orwellian themes, so I decided to check it out. And boy was it worth it.

The core gameplay mechanic is quite interesting and works really well to compliment the engaging story. Some interface quality-of-life features would be nice, but overall it's a very enjoyable experience.

Orwell is a point-and-click game where you are Big Brother, and it's your job to screw people over! Basically, you are tasked with scouring the internet for information about high-risk individuals who could be terrorists. Choices matter and there is a TON of reading, so be prepared!

The game does an excellent job of showing how manipulating small snippets of information can completely change the story to fit your own narrative. The story is well thought out, and the choices you make throughout the story can definitely creep you out. Many times, I found myself asking, "Does the government REALLY need to know this?" It can be startling to realize just how invasive you have to be in this story, and even if it is for the good of the people, it still feels gross.

My biggest complaints:
- There is no manual saving and loading.
- In order to choose chapters (or basically replay a chapter), you have to complete the entire story first. So on the first playthrough, you're really stuck with whatever choices you made.
- The phone calls and chats take FOREVER. Seriously, there should be a way to adjust speed or skip to the end.
- The conflicting information choices sometimes feel a bit shallow or non-sensical, but some outcomes really hinge on these choices.

The key word about this game is atmosphere. I'm a fan of the game's subject: mass surveillance and privacy. If you read '1984' by Georges Orwell and liked it, you'll probably like the ambience of this game.
This small game is all about story telling through text (you need to read a lot). The writing style is really good, modern and easy to understand.
You play the role of an data analyst who will track some "suspicious" people and you upload any data that may be useful to investigators working with you in the game.

Pros:

- The story is interesting and, depending on how you play, it can also have some suspense moments
- The world is believable. The game encourages you to read everything, even bits that are completely optional
- The writing style is great (I played in English)
- I enjoyed the soundtrack. The music is mainly for ambience and works well with the dynamics of the game
- UI: critical point in this kind of game. It is actually intuitive, well designed
- IRL integration: the game has you creating a profile. If you give your real email address, the game will actually send you email requesting your intervention... Perfect for immersion ;-)
- Replayability: this is a game you need to do multiple times to fully experience everything (HOWEVER, I didn't do it and I explain why in the cons below)


Cons:

- The biggest one for me: sometimes, you will want to submit some data you think are relevant, but the game won't let you do that (even though you are a data analyst, the machine decides what you can upload or can't)
- A lot of characters mentioned in the story are useless. I wish their stories and personalities would be more developed to add more complexity to the game and, ultimately, in your decisions. The main folks are very well developed though, for the most part (some are clichés)
- Replayability: once you finish the game, you will want to replay it. However, once knowing where the key choices you will make would really have an impact, I can't bother redoing the whole story just to see other choices
- Lenght: I finished the game in 4 hours. This is really short and I wish it would be longer (for example, 'This is the police' is doing much better on this point)
- DLCs: extending the game lenght by proposing paid DLC suck. Besides, they are not worth the price (currently the same price as the full game)

I recommend this game and I think 10€ (current price) is a good price for it. I'm happy I played it, but I will probably never play it again.
